name: v3.1.0
body:
This release fixes multiple soundness and zero-knowledge issues in the RISC Zero zkVM proof system. The most critical lets an attacker who holds one valid Groth16 receipt have an arbitrary claim accepted; the others range in severity from high to minor. All are fixed together in `risc0-zkvm` 3.1.0, and every receipt format (composite, succinct, Groth16 and on-chain) is affected by at least one of them. **Upgrade to 3.1.0 and regenerate any receipts you rely on.** There is no workaround.

Advisories: [GHSA-g6qg-9j8p-7j87](https://github.com/risc0/risc0/security/advisories/GHSA-g6qg-9j8p-7j87) (risc0), [GHSA-qvmf-qrrq-p2w4](https://github.com/risc0/zirgen/security/advisories/GHSA-qvmf-qrrq-p2w4) (zirgen) and [GHSA-mm6c-35cm-g4x2](https://github.com/risc0/risc0-ethereum/security/advisories/GHSA-mm6c-35cm-g4x2) (risc0-ethereum).

## Security fixes

### 1. Groth16 receipt claim substitution

The RISC Zero Groth16 verifier accepted a Groth16 receipt whose claim digest had been substituted with the digest of a different, attacker-chosen `ReceiptClaim`. An attacker who could produce one valid Groth16 receipt could therefore have an arbitrary claim, including its image ID, journal and exit code, accepted under the same control root.

The root cause is two under-constrained bit decompositions on the path from the proof to the public claim-digest limbs:

- In the Groth16 wrapper circuit (`stark_verify.circom`), the 32 output limbs that are packed into the public claim-digest inputs were not range-checked, so a non-canonical limb decomposition could encode a different digest.
- In the recursion circuit, `BIT_AND_ELEM` decomposed each input into 31 bits and only checked the recomposition modulo the Baby Bear prime, so every input below 2^31 - P had a second valid decomposition. The recursion programs use this operation to split claim fields and digests into 16-bit halves before hashing them, so a prover could alter the claim digest they compute.

### 2. Poseidon254 S-box was not a permutation

The Poseidon hash over the BN254 scalar field, used inside the Groth16 wrapper to verify the final recursion proof, used `x^8` as its S-box. Since `gcd(8, r - 1) != 1`, this map is 8-to-1 rather than a permutation, so inputs differing by an 8th root of unity collide for free. This breaks the collision resistance of the hash and therefore the Merkle commitments and Fiat-Shamir transcript of the STARK that the Groth16 proof verifies. The S-box is now `x^7`.

### 3. A trace could contain more than one execution

The rv32im circuit marks the start of an execution with an `isFirstCycle` row but did not limit how many such rows a trace may contain. Because the memory argument identifies values only by address, timestamp and value, a prover could place two executions in one trace and have a memory read in one execution return a value written by the other. This let a prover skip a guest's own input validation, for example a signature or factorization check, and obtain an accepted receipt for an output no honest execution produces. The circuit now carries a public trace-length value, requires the row before every first cycle to be the last row of the trace, and every verifier checks that value against the proof's size, so a trace holds exactly one execution.

### 4. Host-supplied words were not range-checked

In the rv32im circuit, the words a guest reads from the host through `sys_read` were written to memory without checking that each half fits in 16 bits, which the memory argument assumes. A malicious prover could inject non-canonical memory values that later arithmetic treats inconsistently. Each half-word is now constrained to 16 bits.

### 5. Recursion prover zero-knowledge noise lacked entropy

The recursion prover filled its zero-knowledge padding rows with a single random field element repeated across every cell instead of independent random values. This weakened the zero-knowledge property of succinct and Groth16 receipts; it does not affect soundness.

## Upgrading

- **Receipts.** The rv32im and recursion circuits are regenerated (`risc0-circuit-rv32im` 4.1.0, `risc0-circuit-recursion` 4.1.0), the rv32im seal format and circuit identifier changed, and the control root is new. Receipts produced by earlier versions do not verify under 3.1.0, and receipts from 3.1.0 do not verify under earlier versions; regenerate them.
- **Groth16.** A new trusted setup, 2026-10-20.1, with a new verifying key (`risc0-groth16` 3.0.6). Without CUDA, the shrink-wrap runs the Docker image `risczero/risc0-groth16-prover:v2026-10-20.1`. With CUDA, it needs the `risc0-groth16` 0.2.0 rzup component: `rzup install risc0-groth16`.
- **On-chain verification.** A new `RiscZeroGroth16Verifier` (version 3.1.0, selector `0xe71e6620`) is deployed and routed through the `RiscZeroVerifierRouter` on all supported chains; see GHSA-mm6c-35cm-g4x2. The previous verifiers will be emergency-stopped after a suitable delay for updates.
- **Tooling.** Install with `rzup install cargo-risczero 3.1.0` and `rzup install r0vm 3.1.0`, and use `r0vm` 3.1.0 with `risc0-zkvm` 3.1.0: an older `r0vm` proves with the old circuits.
- **Earlier versions.** All earlier versions of the affected crates will be yanked from crates.io after a suitable delay for updates.

## Crate versions

- `risc0-zkvm`, `risc0-r0vm`, `cargo-risczero`: 3.1.0
- `risc0-circuit-rv32im`, `risc0-circuit-rv32im-sys`, `risc0-circuit-recursion`, `risc0-circuit-recursion-sys`, `risc0-circuit-recursion-zkrs`, `risc0-circuit-recursion-control-zkrs`, `risc0-circuit-keccak`, `risc0-circuit-keccak-sys`: 4.1.0
- `risc0-zkp`, `risc0-binfmt`, `risc0-groth16`: 3.0.6
- `risc0-build`: 3.0.7
- `risc0-sys`: 1.5.1
- `risc0-tools`: 2.0.1
- `risc0-povw`: 0.4.4

The circuits are generated from [zirgen v3.1.0](https://github.com/risc0/zirgen/tree/v3.1.0).

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/risc0/risc0/compare/v3.0.6...v3.1.0
